title: Compound Interest
text:
Compound Interest — Simple vs. compound growth
Imagine you invest $1,000 and earn 10% per year.

- With **simple** growth, you'd earn $100 every year — always 10% of the original $1,000.
- With **compounding**, year one earns $100 (now $1,100). Year two earns 10% of $1,100, which is $110 (now $1,210). Year three earns 10% of $1,210, and so on. Each year's gain is larger than the last, because you're earning on a bigger and bigger balance.

The gap between the two starts small and grows dramatically over time.

title: Compound Interest
text:
Compound Interest — Why time is the key ingredient
Compounding rewards patience more than anything else. The longer your money stays invested, the more compounding cycles it goes through, and the later cycles are the largest. This is why starting early matters so much: someone who begins investing at 25 can end up with more than someone who invests more money but starts at 35, simply because their money had ten extra years to compound.

title: Compound Interest
text:
Compound Interest — The Rule of 72
A quick mental shortcut: divide 72 by your annual return rate to estimate how many years it takes to double your money. At 8% per year, 72 ÷ 8 = about 9 years to double. At 6%, about 12 years. It's an approximation, but a handy one.

title: Compound Interest
text:
Compound Interest — What this means in practice
- Start as early as you can, even with small amounts.
- Leave investments to grow rather than cashing out early.
- Reinvest returns (like dividends) so they can compound too.

title: Compound Interest
text:
Compound Interest — Key takeaways
- Compound interest means earning returns on your past returns.
- Time is the most important factor — early and consistent beats large but late.
- The Rule of 72 quickly estimates how long money takes to double.

title: Diversification
text:
Diversification — Why it reduces risk
Any single investment can perform badly for reasons specific to it — a company loses a lawsuit, an industry falls out of favor, a region hits hard times. When you hold many investments, one bad outcome is cushioned by the others. This company- or sector-specific risk is called **unsystematic risk**, and diversification is the main tool for reducing it.

title: Diversification
text:
Diversification — What diversification cannot do
Diversification does **not** remove all risk. It cannot protect you from **market risk** (also called systematic risk) — the risk that the whole market falls at once, as happens in a broad downturn. When markets drop broadly, a diversified portfolio usually drops too, just typically less violently than a single concentrated bet.

title: Diversification
text:
Diversification — Ways to diversify
- **Across many companies.** Holding shares in hundreds of companies instead of a handful.
- **Across asset classes.** Mixing stocks, bonds, and cash, which tend to behave differently.
- **Across sectors and regions.** Not putting everything into one industry (like technology) or one country.

title: Diversification
text:
Diversification — The easy path: index funds
For most beginners, the simplest way to diversify is a broad **index fund** — a single fund that holds a tiny slice of hundreds or thousands of companies at once. One purchase gives you instant diversification, which is why index funds are a common starting point for new investors.

title: Diversification
text:
Diversification — Key takeaways
- Diversification spreads money across many investments to reduce company- and sector-specific risk.
- It reduces unsystematic risk but not overall market risk.
- Broad index funds are an easy way to get diversified in a single step.

title: Modern Portfolio Theory Basics
text:
Modern Portfolio Theory Basics — The key insight: diversification is close to a free lunch
MPT's central idea is that the risk of a whole portfolio isn't just the average of its parts. Because different investments don't move in lockstep — when some zig, others zag — combining them can reduce the portfolio's overall swings without necessarily reducing its expected return. This is why MPT is often described as diversification being the closest thing to a "free lunch" in investing: you can lower risk without giving up as much return as you'd expect.

title: Modern Portfolio Theory Basics
text:
Modern Portfolio Theory Basics — Risk and return move together
The second idea is that higher expected returns come with higher risk. There's no mix that gives you high returns with no volatility. Stocks have historically returned more than bonds, but with much bigger ups and downs. Choosing an allocation is really about choosing how much short-term volatility you're willing to accept in exchange for higher expected long-term growth.

title: Modern Portfolio Theory Basics
text:
Modern Portfolio Theory Basics — The efficient frontier (the intuition)
MPT describes an "efficient frontier" — the set of portfolios that offer the best possible expected return for each level of risk. The practical takeaway isn't the curve itself, but the principle: for any level of risk you're comfortable with, a well-diversified mix generally beats a concentrated bet. Piling into a single stock or sector usually means taking on extra risk that isn't rewarded.

title: Modern Portfolio Theory Basics
text:
Modern Portfolio Theory Basics — What this means for planning
- Diversify across asset classes (stocks, bonds, cash) and within them.
- Accept that more expected return means more volatility; choose a mix that matches your comfort and time horizon.
- Don't chase concentrated bets hoping for higher returns without the matching risk.

title: Modern Portfolio Theory Basics
text:
Modern Portfolio Theory Basics — Key takeaways
- MPT's core idea: diversification can reduce risk without proportionally reducing expected return, because assets don't all move together.
- Higher expected return always comes with higher risk.
- For any risk level, a diversified mix generally beats a concentrated one.

title: Risk Tolerance and Asset Allocation
text:
Risk Tolerance and Asset Allocation — What risk tolerance means
Risk tolerance is how much short-term ups and downs you can handle, both financially and emotionally. Someone who would panic and sell during a 20% drop has a lower tolerance than someone who would calmly hold or buy more. It's personal — there's no "right" answer — and being honest about it matters, because a plan you abandon in a downturn is worse than a steadier one you can stick with.

title: Risk Tolerance and Asset Allocation
text:
Risk Tolerance and Asset Allocation — Common allocation frameworks
Financial educators often describe three broad, illustrative frameworks:

- **Conservative** — roughly 25% stocks, 70% bonds, 5% cash. Prioritizes stability; lower expected return, smaller swings.
- **Moderate** — roughly 60% stocks, 40% bonds. A balanced middle that captures growth while bonds cushion the falls.
- **Aggressive** — roughly 85% stocks, 15% bonds. Prioritizes long-term growth; higher expected return, bigger swings.

These are general starting points for education, not personal recommendations.

title: Risk Tolerance and Asset Allocation
text:
Risk Tolerance and Asset Allocation — Why time horizon matters
Time horizon — how long until you need the money — can matter as much as tolerance. A longer horizon can absorb more volatility, because there's time to recover from downturns before you need to spend the money. A short horizon argues for a more conservative mix even for someone with a high risk tolerance, because a badly-timed drop right before the goal leaves no time to bounce back. This is the idea behind target-date funds, which automatically grow more conservative as the goal approaches.

title: Risk Tolerance and Asset Allocation
text:
Risk Tolerance and Asset Allocation — Key takeaways
- Asset allocation is a major driver of both expected return and volatility.
- Conservative, moderate, and aggressive are common illustrative frameworks (roughly 25/60/85% stocks).
- A longer time horizon can justify more stocks; a short horizon argues for a more conservative mix regardless of tolerance.

title: What Is a Stock?
text:
What Is a Stock? — Why companies issue stock
Companies sell stock to raise money. Instead of borrowing from a bank, a company can sell ownership stakes to the public and use that cash to grow — hire people, build products, or expand. In exchange, shareholders get a claim on the company's future success.

title: What Is a Stock?
text:
What Is a Stock? — How investors make (or lose) money
There are two main ways a stock can put money in your pocket:

- **Price appreciation.** If the company becomes more valuable, the price of each share can rise, and you can sell for more than you paid. If the company struggles, the price can fall, and you can lose money.
- **Dividends.** Some companies share a portion of their profits with shareholders as regular cash payments called dividends. Not all companies pay them.

There is no guarantee of either. A stock's price can go up or down for many reasons, and a company can reduce or stop paying dividends at any time.

title: What Is a Stock?
text:
What Is a Stock? — The risk of owning individual stocks
Owning a single company's stock ties your money to that one company's fate. If that business does poorly, your investment can lose significant value — even go to zero if the company fails. This company-specific risk is one reason many beginners choose diversified funds, which spread money across many companies, rather than betting on a single stock.

title: What Is a Stock?
text:
What Is a Stock? — Common vs. preferred stock
Most everyday investors buy **common stock**, which usually comes with voting rights at shareholder meetings and the potential for dividends. **Preferred stock** typically has no voting rights but gets priority for dividend payments. Beginners mostly encounter common stock.

title: What Is a Stock?
text:
What Is a Stock? — Key takeaways
- A stock is partial ownership of a company.
- You can earn money through price appreciation and dividends, but neither is guaranteed.
- Individual stocks carry company-specific risk; diversification helps manage it.

title: Moving Averages and Trends
text:
Moving Averages and Trends — What a moving average is
A 50-day moving average is simply the average closing price over the last 50 trading days, recalculated each day. Because it averages many days together, it moves more slowly and smoothly than the daily price. The 50-day average reflects the medium-term trend; the 200-day average reflects the long-term trend.

title: Moving Averages and Trends
text:
Moving Averages and Trends — Reading the trend
When the current price is above its moving average, the stock has generally been rising; when it's below, it has generally been falling. Comparing the two averages adds context: when the 50-day average is above the 200-day average, the medium-term trend is stronger than the long-term one, often described as an uptrend. The reverse — 50-day below 200-day — is often described as a downtrend. When they're close together and the price is drifting, the stock is roughly sideways.

title: Moving Averages and Trends
text:
Moving Averages and Trends — An important caution
Moving averages describe the *past*. They summarize where a price has been, not where it's going. A stock in an uptrend can reverse, and one in a downtrend can recover. Trends are context, not predictions — they help you understand a stock's recent behavior, not forecast its future.

title: Moving Averages and Trends
text:
Moving Averages and Trends — Key takeaways
- A moving average is the average price over a window (e.g. 50 or 200 days), smoothing out daily noise.
- Price above its average and 50-day above 200-day generally indicate an uptrend; the opposite indicates a downtrend.
- Moving averages summarize the past; they do not predict future prices.

title: Reading a Stock Quote
text:
Reading a Stock Quote — Price and daily change
The price is the most recent amount a share traded for. The daily change — shown as a dollar amount and a percentage — compares it to the previous day's closing price. A green +1.5% means the stock is up one and a half percent since yesterday's close; red means it's down.

title: Reading a Stock Quote
text:
Reading a Stock Quote — Day's range
The day's range shows the lowest and highest prices the stock has traded at so far today. A wide range means the price is bouncing around a lot (more volatile today); a narrow range means it's relatively steady.

title: Reading a Stock Quote
text:
Reading a Stock Quote — 52-week range
The 52-week range is the lowest and highest price over the past year. It gives context for today's price: a stock near its 52-week high has climbed a lot recently, while one near its 52-week low has fallen. It doesn't tell you whether the stock is "cheap" or "expensive" in value terms — just where it sits versus its own recent history.

title: Reading a Stock Quote
text:
Reading a Stock Quote — Volume
Volume is how many shares changed hands. Comparing today's volume to the average daily volume tells you whether trading is unusually busy. High volume often accompanies big news, because more people are reacting to it.

title: Reading a Stock Quote
text:
Reading a Stock Quote — P/E ratio
The price-to-earnings (P/E) ratio divides the share price by the company's earnings per share. It roughly answers "how much am I paying for each dollar of the company's annual profit?" A P/E of 20 means investors pay $20 per $1 of yearly earnings. A high P/E often signals that investors expect strong future growth; a low P/E can signal modest expectations or an out-of-favor company. P/E is most meaningful when compared to similar companies, not in isolation.

title: Reading a Stock Quote
text:
Reading a Stock Quote — Key takeaways
- Price and daily change show the latest value and how it moved since yesterday.
- Day's range and 52-week range give short- and long-term context.
- Volume signals how active trading is; the P/E ratio signals how richly a stock is priced relative to its earnings.

title: What Moves Stock Prices
text:
What Moves Stock Prices — Company earnings and news
The biggest company-specific driver is earnings — how much profit a company reports, usually every three months. Prices often move sharply after an earnings report, and not just on the raw numbers but on how they compare to *expectations*. A company can post record profits and still see its stock fall if investors expected even more. Other company news moves prices too: new products, leadership changes, lawsuits, or big contracts.

title: What Moves Stock Prices
text:
What Moves Stock Prices — Macroeconomic news
Broad economic forces move most stocks at once. Interest-rate decisions, inflation reports, employment data, and economic growth figures all shift how investors feel about the future. For example, when interest rates rise, borrowing gets more expensive and future profits are worth less today, which often pressures stock prices across the board.

title: What Moves Stock Prices
text:
What Moves Stock Prices — Market sentiment
Beyond the numbers, prices reflect emotion and expectation — collectively called sentiment. Fear can drive selling even when a company's fundamentals haven't changed, and optimism can lift prices on hope alone. Sentiment is why prices can swing more than the underlying facts seem to justify, and why short-term moves are notoriously hard to predict.

title: What Moves Stock Prices
text:
What Moves Stock Prices — Why short-term moves are hard to predict
Because prices already reflect everything investors currently know, what moves them next is *new* information — which by definition isn't knowable in advance. This is why no one can reliably forecast day-to-day prices, and why long-term investing tends to focus on fundamentals rather than short-term timing.

title: What Moves Stock Prices
text:
What Moves Stock Prices — Key takeaways
- Prices are set by supply and demand, moment to moment.
- Day-to-day, the biggest drivers are earnings (vs. expectations), macroeconomic news, and market sentiment.
- Short-term price movements are very hard to predict because they depend on new, unknowable information.

title: 401(k) Plans and Employer Match
text:
401(k) Plans and Employer Match — Traditional and Roth 401(k)s
Many plans offer both flavors. A Traditional 401(k) uses pre-tax contributions (a tax break now, taxed on withdrawal), while a Roth 401(k) uses after-tax contributions (tax-free qualified withdrawals later). Some people split contributions between the two.

title: 401(k) Plans and Employer Match
text:
401(k) Plans and Employer Match — The employer match
Many employers match a portion of what you contribute — for example, adding money up to a percentage of your salary. This match is effectively additional compensation for saving. Because it's extra money you only get if you contribute, financial educators often describe capturing the full match as one of the highest-priority moves in personal finance: not contributing enough to get the full match leaves guaranteed money on the table.

title: 401(k) Plans and Employer Match
text:
401(k) Plans and Employer Match — Vesting
Employer-matched money sometimes comes with a *vesting* schedule — you may need to stay with the employer for a certain period before the matched funds are fully yours. Your own contributions are always yours immediately.

title: 401(k) Plans and Employer Match
text:
401(k) Plans and Employer Match — Early withdrawals
Because 401(k)s are meant for retirement, withdrawing before the qualifying age generally triggers income tax plus an additional penalty, with limited exceptions. The specifics change and depend on your situation, so verify at IRS.gov.

title: 401(k) Plans and Employer Match
text:
401(k) Plans and Employer Match — Key takeaways
- A 401(k) is an employer retirement account, available in Traditional (pre-tax) and Roth (after-tax) forms.
- An employer match is essentially free money for contributing — capturing the full match is a common top priority.
- Matched funds may vest over time; early withdrawals usually incur tax and a penalty. Verify current rules at IRS.gov.

title: 529 Education Savings Plans
text:
529 Education Savings Plans — How the tax benefit works
Money in a 529 grows without being taxed year to year, and withdrawals are tax-free when used for qualified education expenses — such as college tuition, fees, room and board, and, within limits, some K-12 tuition. The federal government doesn't offer a deduction for contributions, but many states offer their own state-tax deduction or credit for residents who contribute.

title: 529 Education Savings Plans
text:
529 Education Savings Plans — Qualified vs. non-qualified withdrawals
The tax-free benefit applies only to qualified education expenses. If you withdraw money for something else, the earnings portion is generally taxed as income and may face an additional penalty. The contributions you put in (which were already taxed) aren't penalized — only the growth.

title: 529 Education Savings Plans
text:
529 Education Savings Plans — Flexibility features
529 plans have grown more flexible over time. Features can include changing the beneficiary to another family member, and — subject to conditions and limits — options to repurpose unused funds. Because these provisions change, confirm what's currently allowed at IRS.gov.

title: 529 Education Savings Plans
text:
529 Education Savings Plans — Key takeaways
- A 529 plan offers tax-free growth and withdrawals for qualified education expenses.
- No federal deduction, but many states offer one for residents.
- Non-qualified withdrawals are taxed and may be penalized on the earnings; rules change — verify at IRS.gov.

title: Capital Gains and Dividends
text:
Capital Gains and Dividends — Capital gains: short-term vs. long-term
A capital gain is the profit when you sell an investment for more than you paid. How long you held it matters a lot:

- **Short-term** gains (on investments held roughly a year or less) are generally taxed at your ordinary income tax rate — the same as your paycheck.
- **Long-term** gains (on investments held longer) are generally taxed at lower, preferential rates.

This is why holding period matters: selling too soon can turn a lower long-term rate into a higher ordinary one. If you sell for less than you paid, that's a capital loss, which can offset gains (see tax-loss harvesting).

title: Capital Gains and Dividends
text:
Capital Gains and Dividends — Dividends: qualified vs. ordinary
A dividend is a share of company profits paid to shareholders. For taxes, dividends split into:

- **Qualified** dividends, which meet certain requirements and are generally taxed at the lower long-term capital-gains rates.
- **Ordinary (non-qualified)** dividends, taxed at your regular income rate.

title: Capital Gains and Dividends
text:
Capital Gains and Dividends — Why this matters for account choice
Because taxable accounts generate this yearly tax drag, many people prefer to hold their most heavily-taxed investments inside tax-advantaged accounts, and use taxable accounts for more tax-efficient holdings. This idea is called "asset location."

title: Capital Gains and Dividends
text:
Capital Gains and Dividends — Key takeaways
- Capital gains are taxed by holding period: short-term at ordinary rates, long-term at lower rates.
- Dividends split into qualified (lower rates) and ordinary (regular rates).
- Tax-advantaged accounts shelter this activity; specific rates change yearly — verify at IRS.gov.

title: Health Savings Accounts (HSA)
text:
Health Savings Accounts (HSA) — The triple tax advantage
An HSA gets favorable tax treatment at all three stages, which is unusual:

1. **Going in** — contributions are tax-deductible (or pre-tax through payroll), lowering taxable income.
2. **Growing** — the money grows without being taxed year to year.
3. **Coming out** — withdrawals for qualified medical expenses are tax-free.

Most accounts give you a break at only one or two of these stages; the HSA offers all three for medical spending.

title: Health Savings Accounts (HSA)
text:
Health Savings Accounts (HSA) — Why some treat it as a retirement account
HSA funds roll over year to year — they aren't "use it or lose it" — and the account stays with you even if you change jobs or health plans. Because of the triple advantage, some people pay current medical costs out of pocket and let the HSA grow invested for later, treating it as a supplemental retirement account for future medical expenses. After a certain age, non-medical withdrawals are treated more like a Traditional retirement account (taxed as income rather than penalized).

title: Health Savings Accounts (HSA)
text:
Health Savings Accounts (HSA) — Important conditions
The triple tax benefit applies to *qualified* medical expenses; non-qualified withdrawals can be taxed and penalized. You must be enrolled in a qualifying high-deductible plan to contribute. These rules change and depend on your situation — verify at IRS.gov.

title: Health Savings Accounts (HSA)
text:
Health Savings Accounts (HSA) — Key takeaways
- An HSA offers a triple tax advantage: deductible in, tax-free growth, tax-free out for medical costs.
- Requires a qualifying high-deductible health plan; funds roll over and stay with you.
- Some use it as a long-term investment account for future medical expenses. Verify eligibility and limits at IRS.gov.

title: IRAs Explained
text:
IRAs Explained — Traditional and Roth IRAs
Like 401(k)s, IRAs come in two tax flavors. A Traditional IRA may offer a tax deduction on contributions today, with withdrawals taxed as ordinary income later. A Roth IRA takes after-tax money now and offers tax-free qualified withdrawals in retirement. Whether you can deduct a Traditional IRA contribution, or contribute directly to a Roth, can depend on your income and whether you have a workplace plan.

title: IRAs Explained
text:
IRAs Explained — IRA vs. 401(k)
The accounts share the same Traditional/Roth tax logic but differ in structure:

- A **401(k)** is offered by an employer, may include a match, and usually has higher contribution limits.
- An **IRA** is opened on your own through a brokerage, has no employer match, typically has a lower contribution limit, but often offers a wider range of investment choices.

Many people use both: contributing to a 401(k) at least enough to get the employer match, then adding an IRA for more flexibility.

title: IRAs Explained
text:
IRAs Explained — Withdrawal rules
IRAs are designed for retirement, so withdrawing early generally triggers income tax plus a penalty, with certain exceptions. Traditional and Roth accounts also differ in required withdrawals later in life. These rules change and depend on your situation — check IRS.gov.

title: IRAs Explained
text:
IRAs Explained — Key takeaways
- An IRA is a self-opened retirement account, available in Traditional (pre-tax) and Roth (after-tax) forms.
- Compared with a 401(k): no employer match, usually lower limits, but more investment choice.
- Deductibility, income limits, and withdrawal rules change yearly — verify at IRS.gov.

title: Tax-Loss Harvesting and Tax Diversification
text:
Tax-Loss Harvesting and Tax Diversification — Tax-loss harvesting
When an investment in a taxable account is worth less than you paid, selling it "realizes" a capital loss. Those losses can offset capital gains elsewhere, and a limited amount of net loss can offset ordinary income in a year, with the rest carried forward to future years. Deliberately realizing losses to reduce your tax bill is called tax-loss harvesting.

The main rule to know is the **wash-sale rule**: if you buy the same or a "substantially identical" investment shortly before or after selling at a loss, the tax benefit is disallowed. This is why harvesting is done carefully, often by moving into a similar-but-not-identical investment. Loss thresholds and the exact rules change — check IRS.gov.

title: Tax-Loss Harvesting and Tax Diversification
text:
Tax-Loss Harvesting and Tax Diversification — Tax diversification
Tax diversification means spreading your savings across the three tax treatments — tax-deferred, Roth/tax-free, and taxable — rather than putting everything in one. Because no one knows their future tax rates or what tax law will look like decades from now, holding a mix gives you options in retirement: you can choose which account to draw from to manage your taxable income year by year.

title: Tax-Loss Harvesting and Tax Diversification
text:
Tax-Loss Harvesting and Tax Diversification — Asset location
A related idea is "asset location": placing your least tax-efficient investments (those that generate lots of taxable income) inside tax-advantaged accounts, and more tax-efficient ones in taxable accounts. It's about *which account* holds *which investment*, to reduce overall tax drag.

title: Tax-Loss Harvesting and Tax Diversification
text:
Tax-Loss Harvesting and Tax Diversification — Key takeaways
- Tax-loss harvesting realizes losses to offset gains and some income; watch the wash-sale rule.
- Tax diversification spreads savings across deferred, Roth, and taxable accounts for future flexibility.
- Asset location puts tax-inefficient holdings in sheltered accounts. All rules change yearly — verify at IRS.gov.

title: Taxable Brokerage Accounts
text:
Taxable Brokerage Accounts — What "taxable" means
Unlike a 401(k) or IRA, a brokerage account gives no deduction and no tax-free growth. Instead you pay tax as you go: on dividends and interest each year, and on capital gains when you sell an investment for a profit. The trade-off for this ongoing tax is freedom.

title: Taxable Brokerage Accounts
text:
Taxable Brokerage Accounts — The flexibility advantage
Taxable accounts have no contribution limits — you can invest as much as you want. There are no early-withdrawal penalties and no required withdrawals later in life; the money is available any time for any purpose. That makes a brokerage account well-suited to goals before retirement, or as a supplement once tax-advantaged accounts are full.

title: Taxable Brokerage Accounts
text:
Taxable Brokerage Accounts — Where it fits in the usual priority order
A common educational framework for ordering savings is: contribute to a 401(k) at least enough to capture any employer match, then fund tax-advantaged accounts like IRAs and HSAs, and use a taxable brokerage account for anything beyond that or for goals you'll reach before retirement age. This is a general framework, not personalized advice.

title: Taxable Brokerage Accounts
text:
Taxable Brokerage Accounts — Tax efficiency
Because brokerage accounts are taxed yearly, being tax-aware helps: holding investments long enough for long-term capital-gains rates, favoring tax-efficient funds, and using capital losses to offset gains all reduce the tax drag.

title: Taxable Brokerage Accounts
text:
Taxable Brokerage Accounts — Key takeaways
- A taxable brokerage account has no special tax treatment: taxed on dividends, interest, and realized gains.
- In exchange it offers full flexibility — no contribution limits, penalties, or required withdrawals.
- Often used after tax-advantaged accounts are full, or for pre-retirement goals.

title: Traditional vs. Roth
text:
Traditional vs. Roth — Traditional: a tax break now
Traditional contributions are usually made with pre-tax money — you may deduct them from your taxable income today, lowering this year's tax bill. The money grows tax-deferred, and you pay ordinary income tax on withdrawals in retirement. Traditional accounts often appeal to people who expect to be in a lower tax bracket later than they are now.

title: Traditional vs. Roth
text:
Traditional vs. Roth — Roth: a tax break later
Roth contributions are made with after-tax money — no deduction today. In return, qualified withdrawals in retirement, including all the growth, are completely tax-free. Roth accounts often appeal to people who expect to be in the same or a higher tax bracket later, or who simply value the certainty of tax-free income in retirement.

title: Traditional vs. Roth
text:
Traditional vs. Roth — The core trade-off
The decision hinges on a comparison you can't make with certainty: your tax rate now versus in retirement.

- If your rate will be **lower** in retirement, Traditional's up-front deduction tends to win.
- If your rate will be **higher** (or you want certainty), Roth's tax-free withdrawals tend to win.

Because the future is unknown, many people hold both to hedge.

title: Traditional vs. Roth
text:
Traditional vs. Roth — Other differences to know
Roth IRAs have income limits that can restrict who may contribute directly, and the two types differ on required withdrawals later in life. These rules change, so confirm the current specifics at IRS.gov or with a tax professional.

title: Traditional vs. Roth
text:
Traditional vs. Roth — Key takeaways
- Traditional = deduct now, pay tax on withdrawal; Roth = no deduction now, tax-free qualified withdrawals.
- The choice depends on your tax rate now vs. later — unknowable, so many hold both.
- Income limits and withdrawal rules apply and change yearly; verify at IRS.gov.

title: The Three Tax Treatments
text:
The Three Tax Treatments — 1. Tax-deferred (pay taxes later)
With a tax-deferred account, you often deduct contributions from your income today, so you pay less tax now. Your money then grows without being taxed year to year, and you pay ordinary income tax when you withdraw it later — typically in retirement. Traditional 401(k)s and Traditional IRAs work this way. The idea: get a tax break now, pay tax on the way out.

title: The Three Tax Treatments
text:
The Three Tax Treatments — 2. Tax-free / Roth (pay taxes now)
With a Roth account, you contribute money you've already paid tax on, so there's no deduction today. In exchange, your money grows and — if you follow the rules — comes out completely tax-free in retirement, including all the investment growth. Roth 401(k)s and Roth IRAs work this way. The idea: pay tax now, owe nothing later.

title: The Three Tax Treatments
text:
The Three Tax Treatments — 3. Taxable (pay as you go)
A regular taxable brokerage account gets no special tax treatment. There are no contribution limits and no withdrawal penalties, but you pay tax along the way — on dividends and interest each year, and on capital gains when you sell an investment for a profit.

title: The Three Tax Treatments
text:
The Three Tax Treatments — Why it matters: tax diversification
Because no one knows their future tax rate, many people spread money across more than one treatment — some tax-deferred, some Roth, some taxable. This "tax diversification" gives flexibility to manage taxes in retirement.

title: The Three Tax Treatments
text:
The Three Tax Treatments — Key takeaways
- Tax-deferred: deduct now, pay ordinary tax on withdrawal (Traditional 401(k)/IRA).
- Roth/tax-free: no deduction now, tax-free qualified withdrawals (Roth 401(k)/IRA).
- Taxable: no special treatment, taxed as you go (brokerage accounts).
- Specific limits and rules change yearly — verify at IRS.gov.
